disclaimer: These suggestions are general gardening advice, not a guarantee. Always read and follow the label of any product, check what is approved in your country, and ask your local agriculture office or plant nursery if you are unsure. Try the simple, non-chemical steps first.

diseases.symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves, later turning dark and scabby. Fruit can get rough dark scabs.
treatment: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves, where the fungus survives the winter
Prune to open up the tree so leaves dry quickly
Remove badly spotted leaves and fruit
If needed, spray a protectant fungicide (for example sulfur or captan) from early spring, following the product label
prevention: Choose scab-resistant apple varieties
Clean up fallen leaves every autumn
Water at the base of the tree, not over the leaves

diseases.symptoms: Round brown leaf spots with a purple edge (a 'frog-eye' look), rotting fruit and dead, sunken areas on branches.
treatment: Prune out dead wood and cankers on branches, cutting into healthy wood, and destroy them
Remove rotten and shrivelled fruit from the tree and the ground
If needed, use a fungicide labelled for apple black rot, following the product label
prevention: Remove dead branches and old fruit each season
Avoid wounding the bark
Keep the tree well watered and fed so it stays strong

diseases.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper side of leaves, sometimes with small tube-like growths underneath.
treatment: Remove badly affected leaves
Remove nearby juniper or cedar trees if possible, since the fungus needs them to complete its life cycle
If needed, use a fungicide labelled for apple rust from early spring, following the product label
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Avoid planting apples close to junipers or cedars

diseases.symptoms: The leaf looks normal: even green colour, no spots, mould or damage.
treatment: No treatment needed. Your plant looks healthy.
prevention: Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves
Remove fallen leaves and plant debris regularly
Check the leaves once a week for early spots, mould or pests

diseases.symptoms: White powdery patches on leaves, which may curl, twist or turn yellow.
treatment: Remove and bin badly affected leaves and shoots
Prune to improve air flow around the tree
Spray a potassium bicarbonate solution, neem oil or sulfur, following the product label
Repeat sprays every 7 to 14 days while the weather stays humid
prevention: Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser, which causes soft new growth
Keep branches open and not crowded
Water at the base, in the morning

diseases.symptoms: Long, narrow, rectangular grey or tan spots that run between the leaf veins, mostly on lower leaves.
treatment: Remove and destroy badly affected lower leaves
Clear away old corn residue after harvest
In severe cases, use a fungicide labelled for corn, following the product label
prevention: Rotate crops so corn does not follow corn
Choose resistant varieties
Space plants so air can move between them

diseases.symptoms: Small round to oval reddish-brown powdery bumps on both sides of the leaves.
treatment: Light infections usually do little harm, so keep watching the plants
Remove badly affected leaves
In severe cases, use a fungicide labelled for corn, following the product label
prevention: Plant rust-resistant varieties
Plant early in the season
Avoid overcrowding

diseases.symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions, often several centimetres long, on the leaves.
treatment: Remove and destroy badly affected leaves
Clear away old corn residue after harvest
In severe cases, use a fungicide labelled for corn, following the product label
prevention: Rotate crops
Choose resistant varieties
Avoid overhead watering

diseases.symptoms: Brown leaf spots with dark borders, and berries that shrivel into hard black 'mummies'.
treatment: Remove and destroy all mummified berries and infected leaves
Prune the vine so sunlight and air reach the fruit
If needed, use a fungicide labelled for grape black rot from early shoot growth, following the product label
prevention: Clean up fallen fruit and leaves every season
Train vines to be open and airy
Avoid overhead watering

diseases.symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' yellow and brown patterns on leaves, and dark spots on berries. It is a disease of the wood.
treatment: There is no cure, so protect the rest of the vineyard or vines
Prune out affected wood in dry weather, well below the damage, and burn or bin it
If a vine is badly affected, remove it
Disinfect pruning tools between cuts
prevention: Prune only in dry weather
Protect large pruning wounds
Avoid stressing vines with drought

diseases.symptoms: Dark brown, irregular spots on leaves, which can make them dry out and drop early.
treatment: Remove and destroy affected leaves and fallen debris
Prune to improve air flow
If needed, use a fungicide labelled for grape leaf spot, following the product label
prevention: Keep vines open and well spaced
Water at the base of the plant
Clean up fallen leaves

diseases.symptoms: Blotchy yellow mottling on leaves, small lopsided bitter fruit, and a tree that slowly declines.
treatment: There is no cure. Contact your local agriculture office or department for advice, because this disease is serious and spreads between trees
Remove and destroy infected trees as advised by the authorities
Control the Asian citrus psyllid, the insect that spreads it
prevention: Buy only certified disease-free plants
Check new growth for psyllids
Do not move cuttings or plants from infected areas

diseases.symptoms: Small dark spots on leaves that may fall out and leave tiny holes, plus spots and pits on the fruit.
treatment: Remove badly affected leaves and fruit
Spray copper in early spring and at leaf fall, following the product label
Avoid overhead watering
prevention: Choose resistant varieties
Do not over-fertilise with nitrogen
Keep the tree well watered and not stressed

Water at the base, not over the leaves

diseases.symptoms: Brown spots with ring patterns like a target, usually first on the older, lower leaves, with yellowing around them.
treatment: Remove the affected lower leaves
Mulch around the plants to stop soil splashing onto the leaves
If needed, use a fungicide such as copper or chlorothalonil, following the product label
Keep the plants fed and watered, because stressed plants get it worse
prevention: Rotate crops every year
Water at the base of the plants
Use certified, healthy seed potatoes
Clear plant debris after harvest

diseases.symptoms: Dark, water-soaked patches on leaves that spread fast, often with white fuzzy mould on the underside in damp weather. Tubers can rot.
treatment: Act quickly, because this disease spreads very fast in wet weather
Remove and destroy infected plants. Bag them and do not compost them
Protect nearby healthy plants with a fungicide such as copper, following the product label
Do not store tubers from infected plants
prevention: Use certified, healthy seed potatoes
Remove volunteer potato plants
Avoid overhead watering and give plants space
Rotate crops

diseases.symptoms: Tiny yellow dots on leaves, a dusty or bronzed look, and fine webbing on the underside. Leaves dry out and drop.
treatment: Spray the plants with a strong jet of water, especially the underside of leaves
Spray insecticidal soap, neem oil or horticultural oil, covering both sides of the leaves, following the product label
Repeat every 5 to 7 days for a few weeks
Remove very badly infested leaves
prevention: Keep plants watered, because mites love dry, dusty, stressed plants
Check the undersides of leaves regularly in hot weather
Avoid harsh insecticides that kill the helpful insects that eat mites

diseases.symptoms: Brown spots with ring patterns on leaves, similar to early blight, and sometimes spots on the fruit.

prevention: Avoid overhead watering
Rotate crops
Clear plant debris at the end of the season

diseases.symptoms: Leaves curl upwards and turn yellow at the edges, and the plant stays small with few fruit. It is spread by whiteflies.
treatment: There is no cure for the virus
Remove and destroy infected plants. Bag them and do not compost them
Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps, insecticidal soap or neem oil
Cover young plants with fine insect netting
prevention: Choose virus-resistant varieties
Check new plants for whiteflies before planting
Use reflective mulch to deter whiteflies
Remove weeds that shelter whiteflies

diseases.symptoms: Light and dark green mottled patches on leaves, which may be twisted or narrow. Fruit can ripen unevenly.
treatment: There is no cure for the virus
Remove and destroy infected plants. Bag them and do not compost them
Wash your hands with soap and disinfect tools after handling infected plants
Do not smoke or handle tobacco before touching the plants
prevention: Use virus-free seed and resistant varieties
Disinfect tools and pots
Control weeds
Do not plant tomatoes where infected plants grew last season
